strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a critical bottleneck in scientific foundation models: the lack of fine-grained, instance-level textual descriptions in organismal biology compared to general web datasets.

Carefully engineered and scalable synthetic captioning pipeline that effectively grounds MLLM outputs using Wikipedia visual excerpts and taxon-tailored format examples, significantly mitigating hallucination.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 10 zero-shot species classification benchmarks and multiple text-image retrieval tasks, showing consistent and substantial improvements over BioCLIP (+8.8% classification, +21.3% retrieval) and other general/specialized baselines.

Thorough ablation studies verifying key design decisions, including the dual-projector architecture, prompt design, domain-context injection, compute fairness (doubled epoch baseline), and coverage generalization.
Insightful interpretability analyses using Grad-CAM and Finer-CAM demonstrating that the model learns localized associations for anatomical traits and behavioral semantics.
weaknesses: Conceptual and algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited, as the core components (synthetic captioning with LLM/MLLM guidance, prompt conditioning, and dual projection heads for heterogeneous supervision) are established techniques in general-domain vision-language pretraining adapted here to biological data.

The human evaluation panel lacks sufficient domain expertise: out of 16 evaluators, only one is an ecologist while 15 are computer science students, which undermines the reliability of assessing fine-grained diagnostic traits and biological specificity.

Wikipedia visual coverage is relatively modest at the species level (~30%), requiring reliance on genus fallbacks or class examples for a large portion of taxa; deeper error analysis on whether hallucinated genus-level traits propagate to rare species is lacking.

The loss formulation and training dynamics between the two supervision objectives (taxonomy contrastive loss vs. caption contrastive loss) are not sufficiently detailed or ablated in terms of loss weighting and gradient interactions.

strengths: Compelling motivation addressing a critical bottleneck in scientific foundation models: moving beyond sparse symbolic taxonomic labels by injecting rich, trait-grounded natural language supervision into biological representation learning.
Well-designed and scalable data curation pipeline that effectively mitigates MLLM hallucination by combining structured Wikipedia visual attribute extraction with taxon-tailored format prompting.
Impressive empirical improvements: BioCAP outperforms BioCLIP by +8.8% on average across 10 zero-shot species classification benchmarks and by +21.3% on fine-grained biological text-image retrieval.

Rigorous ablation studies and control experiments, including training epoch parity (200 epochs baseline), single vs. dual projector architectures, prompt variations, and generalization performance to species not covered by Wikipedia.

Comprehensive qualitative validation through Grad-CAM, Finer-CAM, and t-SNE visualizations, confirming that the model attends to biologically meaningful diagnostic traits and behavior semantics rather than spurious background correlations.
A well-structured human evaluation measuring groundedness, specificity, completeness, and clarity, complemented by inter-annotator agreement metrics (Gwet's AC1).
weaknesses: The human evaluation relies on 16 participants consisting of only 1 ecologist and 15 computer science students; non-expert annotators may not reliably identify subtle morphological inaccuracies or domain-specific hallucinations.
Dependence on existing encyclopedic knowledge (Wikipedia covers ~30% of unique taxa at the species level), which may limit applicability to extremely rare, undescribed, or poorly documented species.

Architectural and algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental, as dual-projector CLIP contrastive training and MLLM-based synthetic captioning are established paradigms; the novelty resides primarily in the domain-specific data formulation and empirical execution.
No ablation or comparative analysis across different MLLM caption generators (e.g., evaluating whether smaller open-source models or alternative architectures suffice relative to InternVL3 38B).

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem: Most biological foundation models rely strictly on discrete taxonomic names, neglecting the descriptive power of natural language. The paper effectively bridges this gap by introducing instance-level, trait-grounded descriptive captions.

Principled and effective captioning pipeline: Directly prompting MLLMs often leads to fine-grained hallucinations in specialized scientific domains. The proposed combination of automated Wikipedia morphological extraction and taxon-tailored format examples provides effective domain grounding that noticeably curbs hallucination.

Significant and consistent empirical improvements: BIOCAP demonstrates strong gains over BioCLIP across 10 zero-shot classification benchmarks (+8.8% average top-1 accuracy, with standout jumps such as +23.5% on Fungi) and achieves substantial margins on biological retrieval tasks (+21.3% average gain).

Thorough ablations and qualitative analysis: The authors provide detailed ablation studies isolating the effects of prompt styles, external contexts, single vs. dual visual projectors, and compute budgets (200-epoch baseline). Qualitative visualizations (Grad-CAM on fine-grained anatomy and behavior, t-SNE clustering) and human evaluations with inter-rater reliability metrics (Gwet's AC1) further substantiate the claims.
High quality of presentation: The paper is clear, well-structured, and includes comprehensive details in the appendix (exact prompts, licensing, data statistics, and hyperparameter choices).
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core modeling framework relies on standard contrastive learning (CLIP) augmented with a dual visual projector, a technique previously explored in heterogeneous multimodal literature. The main innovation lies in the data-generation pipeline and domain application rather than model architecture.

Incomplete taxonomic coverage from Wikipedia: Directly extracted morphological data from Wikipedia covers only ~29.5% of taxa (and 52.3% of sample images), requiring reliance on genus fallbacks or purely ungrounded format examples for the rest. While Table 4 shows knowledge generalization to uncovered species, this remains an inherent limitation of web-scraping grounding.

Scope of downstream evaluation: The empirical evaluation focuses almost exclusively on zero-shot species classification and image-text retrieval. Assessing linear probing, few-shot transfer, or downstream biodiversity tasks (such as phenotypic trait discovery or ecological niche modeling) would further strengthen the claims of foundation model utility.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in scientific multimodal foundation models: moving beyond sparse categorical taxonomy labels to fine-grained, descriptive language supervision.

Well-motivated and effective data pipeline: leveraging Wikipedia visual traits and taxon-tailored format exemplars effectively mitigates MLLM hallucinations, yielding grounded, trait-specific captions at scale (TreeOfLife-10M).
Decoupled dual-projector design is technically sound and specifically addresses the heterogeneity between concise taxonomic labels and dense descriptive captions.

Impressive empirical improvements: BioCAP outperforms BioCLIP across 10 zero-shot classification benchmarks (+8.8% average top-1 accuracy) and substantially boosts text-image retrieval (+21.9% average across INQUIRE, Cornell Bird, and PlantID).

Thorough ablation and validation suite: comprehensive studies covering prompt variations, context types, MLLM backbones and scales, human evaluation with inter-rater reliability metrics (Gwet's AC1), and visual interpretability analyses (Grad-CAM, Finer-CAM, t-SNE).
weaknesses: Gains do not transfer strongly to downstream few-shot classification (Table 18) and non-classification visual tasks (Table 19), where performance remains largely comparable to BioCLIP, though the authors reasonably analyze this prototype-distraction trade-off.

Generating captions across 10 million images required significant computational expenditure (30 hours across 12 H100 GPUs with InternVL3-38B), which could be a barrier for scaling to larger biological repositories (e.g., TreeOfLife-200M) without pre-released artifacts.

External knowledge coverage is inherently uneven across the tree of life (only ~30% of species have visual descriptions on Wikipedia), requiring fallback to genus-level descriptions or exemplars alone for underrepresented taxa.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in scientific foundation models: the scarcity of instance-level, biologically grounded descriptive text for organismal images beyond simple taxonomic names.

The proposed caption generation framework is well-principled, effectively mitigating MLLM hallucination by injecting verified Wikipedia visual excerpts and taxon-tailored format exemplars into the generation prompt.

Extensive empirical validation demonstrating substantial improvements over existing baselines like BioCLIP across 10 zero-shot species classification benchmarks (+8.8% average top-1 accuracy) and three multimodal retrieval/reranking benchmarks (+21.9% average gain).

Thorough and insightful ablation studies that convincingly demonstrate the necessity of trait-focused prompts, external knowledge injection, and decoupled dual visual projectors for handling heterogeneous text supervision.

Comprehensive qualitative and diagnostic analyses, including human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1), Grad-CAM trait/behavior visual grounding, t-SNE feature visualizations, and rigorous data leakage control using perceptual hashing.
weaknesses: The performance gains on few-shot visual classification (Tables 18 and 20) and general biological visual tasks (Table 19) are modest compared to the zero-shot classification and text-image retrieval benchmarks.
The synthetic caption generation pipeline introduces non-trivial computational overhead (requiring 360 H100 GPU-hours for 10 million images with InternVL3-38B).
Direct species-level Wikipedia visual coverage is limited to roughly 30% of taxa in TreeOfLife-10M, necessitating fallback to genus-level descriptions for many species.
The causal/linear latent variable model presented in Section 3.1 and Appendix A serves primarily as intuitive conceptual motivation rather than providing formal theoretical guarantees.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored challenge in scientific vision foundation models: bridging organismal biological images with natural language beyond sparse taxonomic labels.

Proposes an effective and well-motivated domain-grounded caption generation pipeline, combining Wikipedia morphological trait extraction with taxon-tailored format exemplars to mitigate MLLM hallucination.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation across 10 zero-shot classification benchmarks, natural language retrieval benchmarks (INQUIRE-Rerank, Cornell Bird, PlantID), and few-shot settings, demonstrating substantial performance improvements (e.g., +8.8% average zero-shot top-1 over BioCLIP).
Thorough ablations covering captioning strategies, prompt formulations, number of format examples, MLLM backbone choices/scales, and the dual-projector architecture.
Compelling qualitative and interpretability analyses, including Grad-CAM trait/behavior localization, t-SNE visualizations of semantic spaces, and human evaluation of caption quality.
weaknesses: External knowledge coverage is incomplete: only ~30% of taxa and ~52% of training instances possess species-level visual information on Wikipedia, necessitating genus-level fallbacks or relying purely on format examples.

The human evaluation panel comprises only 1 domain expert (ecologist) alongside 15 computer science students, which somewhat limits the authoritative assessment of fine-grained morphological correctness.

Performance improvements in few-shot classification and non-classification biological vision tasks are relatively modest compared to the prominent gains observed in zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval.

Generating captions for 10M images requires notable compute resources (360 GPU-hours on H100s), which may pose practical constraints when scaling to even larger biodiversity repositories (e.g., TreeOfLife-200M).
